verses.text: Now, brothers, we want you to know about the grace that God has given the churches of Macedonia.
In the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity.
For I testify that they gave according to their ability and even beyond it. Of their own accord,
they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints.
And not only did they do as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us, because it was the will of God.
So we urged Titus to help complete your act of grace, just as he had started it.
But just as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in complete earnestness, and in the love we inspired in you—see that you also excel in this grace of giving.
I am not making a demand, but I am testing the sincerity of your love in comparison to the earnestness of others.
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich.
And this is my opinion about what is helpful for you in this matter: Last year you were the first not only to give, but even to have such a desire.
Now finish the work, so that you may complete it just as eagerly as you began, according to your means.
For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have.
It is not our intention that others may be relieved while you are burdened, but that there may be equality.
At the present time, your surplus will meet their need, so that in turn their surplus will meet your need. Then there will be equality.
As it is written: "He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall."
But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same devotion I have for you.
For not only did he welcome our appeal, but he is eagerly coming to you of his own volition.
Along with Titus we are sending the brother who is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel.
More than that, this brother was chosen by the churches to accompany us with the offering—the gracious gift we administer to honor the Lord Himself and to show our eagerness to help.
We hope to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift.
For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men.
And we are sending along with them our brother whose earnestness has been proven many times and in many ways, and now even more so by his great confidence in you.
As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker among you. As for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, to the glory of Christ.
In full view of the churches, then, show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you.

context.author: Paul the apostle, with Timothy (1:1)
context.genre: Letter, personal and defensive, among Paul’s most emotional
context.audience: The church in Corinth, after a painful period of conflict
context.mapLabel: MACEDONIA, WHERE CHURCHES GAVE OUT OF POVERTY
context.setting: Paul begins the appeal for the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He points to the churches of Macedonia, who gave generously despite deep poverty, and urges the Corinthians to finish what they started a year earlier. He announces Titus’s return with two other brothers.
context.custom: Giving across churches shows unity between Jews and Gentiles. Paul does not command it, and he stresses that gifts should match a person’s means. The Macedonian churches begged for the privilege of giving.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 9 continues with the benefits of cheerful giving.
context.timelineBible: Verse 15 echoes Exodus 16:18, the gathering of manna, “whoever gathered much had no excess, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”
context.sparkNotes: The Macedonian churches gave beyond their means, begging for the privilege. Paul urges the Corinthians to complete the gift, as a test of their love. Jesus Christ, though rich, became poor so that we might become rich. Titus and two others are being sent to handle the money honestly.

translation.meaning: Paul uses it for God’s gift in Christ and for the gift of the collection. The same word describes generosity.
Sharing in common. The collection is called a fellowship in ministry to the saints.

otBackground.note: The manna gathered by each family met their need.

overview.summary: The Macedonian churches gave generously from poverty. Paul urges Corinth to finish its gift, reminds them of Christ who became poor, and arranges honest handling of the money.
overview.settingLine: Paul asks Corinth to finish its gift.

history.t: Macedonia was a Roman province, and Paul says the churches there faced a severe trial and deep poverty (v.2).
Famine struck Judea (Acts 11:28), and believers there were poor.

customs.t: Paul says the abundance of one meets the need of another (v.14), so that there is equality.
Paul has others handle the money so no one can blame him.

archaeology.t: Corinth minted its own bronze coinage, some of which was in circulation in Paul’s day.
Greek inscriptions mention grain shortages in the East during Claudius’s reign.

overview.discussion: Paul uses the generosity of the Macedonians as a model. Who has taught me by example what generous giving looks like?
overview.book: The second letter to the Corinthians · 13 chapters. Paul’s most personal letter, written to heal a strained relationship.
overview.author: Paul

historicalImage.caption: The Gathering of the Manna, by Nicolas Poussin (1637-39). Paul quotes the manna story of Exodus 16 to teach fair sharing between the churches: the one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered little had no lack (2 Corinthians 8:15).
